citeAs: Zayene, M., Endres, J., Havolli, A., Corbière, C., Cherkaoui, S., Kontouli, A., Alahi, A. (2025). HELVIPAD: A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation. arXiv:2411.18335.
creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi (EPFL, Switzerland; TU Darmstadt, Germany)
description: HELVIPAD is a real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 39,553 labeled video frames from 29 video sequences across diverse indoor and outdoor environments (university campus), under varied lighting conditions including day and night. Collected using two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline and a synchronized Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels at 1920×512 pixel resolution, along with an augmented training set with increased label density via depth completion.
name: HELVIPAD
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Projection accuracy was assessed by calculating pixel error between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions, resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels. For visually challenging areas (e.g., object edges), the error was 8.0 pixels. Per-sequence evaluation showed an overall average pixel error of 8.0 pixels (0.40% of image diagonal). Depth completion quality was validated by splitting each LiDAR point cloud into 80/20 train/test sets and computing MAE, RMSE, MARE, and Inlier Ratio metrics; the pipeline achieved MARE of 0.007 and IR of 0.856 on all train sequences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels were generated automatically by projecting LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images. The mapping process involved: (1) selecting key 3D points on a 19×19 chessboard for initial calibration, (2) applying initial rotation/translation transformations, (3) converting to spherical coordinates, (4) optimizing rotation and translation parameters by minimizing reprojection error using BFGS optimization. Disparity values were derived from depth values using the spherical disparity formula. Projection accuracy was validated by manually selecting 200 random LiDAR points and measuring Euclidean distance to image positions (average error: 1.7 pixels; 8.0 pixels for visually challenging areas).
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was collected on a university campus, which may limit generalizability to other urban environments. The depth completion pipeline increases density of low-range depth values (particularly within 0–10 meter range) due to interpolation and removal of out-of-distribution samples, enriching representation of closer objects. LiDAR precision decreases over longer distances, causing exponential decay in pixel percentage with increasing depth. The temporal aggregation approach for depth completion is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. Indoor sequences have lower total point counts than outdoor sequences.
rai:dataCollection: Data was collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps at an initial resolution of 3840×1920 pixels, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor (64 beams, 42.4° vertical FOV, operating at 10 fps) mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. The rig was mounted on a custom-built, remotely controlled robot chassis navigating a university campus. A central processor (NVIDIA Jetson Xavier) managed data capture and ensured device synchronization via hardware-triggered flash synchronization. In total, 29 video sequences were collected across indoor (corridors, halls) and outdoor (squares, external parking, footpaths) settings under various lighting conditions.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of synchronized video streams from two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps (3840×1920 pixels initial resolution) and LiDAR point clouds from an Ouster OS1-64 sensor (64 beams, 10 fps). The dataset includes 29 video sequences with an average duration of 2 minutes and 41 seconds, spanning indoor and outdoor scenes with pedestrians (average 13.33 pedestrians in indoor sequences and 17.65 in outdoor sequences).
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: December 2023 to February 2024 (sequences recorded between 2023-12-06 and 2024-01-27)
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was collected on a university campus, which may not fully represent all real-world environments. LiDAR occlusions were not explicitly handled (though the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact). The depth completion pipeline does not provide labels at object boundaries. The temporal aggregation for depth completion is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. The dataset provides only omnidirectional stereo images and LiDAR point clouds but no odometry information. Night outdoor scenes are underrepresented compared to daytime scenes.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: An augmented training set was created using a depth completion pipeline tailored for 360° images. The pipeline uses temporal aggregation (fusing current frame's point cloud with 4 preceding and 4 succeeding frames), spherical interpolation via k-nearest neighbors (k=17) weighted by inverse distance, and filtering based on uncertainty (relative weighted variance) and out-of-distribution thresholds. This increased the ratio of labeled pixels from approximately 12% to 61%. The augmented set is provided alongside the original sparse labels as an additional training resource.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: LiDAR point clouds were projected onto equirectangular images via an optimization-based mapping algorithm (minimizing reprojection error using BFGS). Camera frames were downsampled from 30 fps to 10 fps (retaining one out of every three frames) to match LiDAR frame rate. Images were cropped to remove unnecessary borders (sky, ground) and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 pixels. Depth values were converted to spherical disparity in degrees. Synchronization was achieved via hardware-triggered flash at the start of each recording session, with a maximum de-synchronization of 16.67 ms.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset captures dynamic human environments with pedestrians, enabling development of depth estimation systems for mobile robots in healthcare, autonomous driving, and agriculture applications. The dataset includes images of pedestrians in public spaces on a university campus, which may raise privacy considerations. The work aims to advance omnidirectional depth estimation for safer robot navigation in human environments.
rai:dataUseCases: Developing and benchmarking omnidirectional stereo depth estimation models; robotic navigation and exploration in complex indoor and outdoor environments; assessing robustness of depth estimation methods to diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges; cross-scene generalization studies; training and evaluating models for 360° stereo matching.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: KISS-ICP (LiDAR odometry algorithm based on ICP) was evaluated for temporal aggregation of point clouds during depth completion, though the simpler 'no movement' aggregation was ultimately used. BFGS optimization algorithm was used for LiDAR-to-image mapping parameter optimization.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains images of pedestrians in public indoor and outdoor spaces on a university campus. Pedestrian counts are recorded per sequence (average 13.33 in indoor, 17.65 in outdoor sequences). No explicit mention of anonymization or consent procedures for individuals captured in the scenes.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: Labels are generated automatically from LiDAR projection; no concept of multiple independent annotations per item applies.
null_reasons.rai:annotatorDemographics: Labels are generated automatically from LiDAR sensor data; no human annotators involved.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Labels are generated automatically via LiDAR projection pipeline; no annotation platform used.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: No explicit discussion of missing data handling beyond the sparse LiDAR coverage addressed by depth completion (which is a manipulation protocol, not missing data handling).
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation of missing values described; depth completion is a label augmentation technique, not imputation of missing sensor readings.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan described in the paper.
